sections.h: Daniel 11: the Seleucids as the king of the north
sections.b: Daniel 11 gives the history of the Seleucid kings in a code of "the king of the north" and "the king of the south" (the Ptolemies of Egypt). Seleucus I rose from Ptolemy's commander (Daniel 11:5). His descendants Antiochus II, Seleucus II, Antiochus III the Great and Seleucus IV appear without names, and the chapter's long second half is about Antiochus IV Epiphanes (Daniel 11:21-35). Antiochus III took Judea from Egypt about 200 BC (Daniel 11:15-16); Rome stopped him at Magnesia in 190 BC (Daniel 11:18). Jews in Judea saw the Seleucid kings as rulers they could not escape, and Daniel 11 is the only place in the Bible that tells their story in order.

sections.h: Daniel 11 and the persecution of 167-164 BC
sections.b: Daniel 11:21-35 matches the persecution that led to the Maccabean revolt, whether it is read as prophecy given in advance or as history written after the event. Antiochus IV's raid on the Temple (Daniel 11:28; 1 Maccabees 1:20-24), his humiliation by Rome at Eleusis in 168 BC (Daniel 11:30), the end of the regular offering and the setting up of the abomination that desolates (Daniel 11:31; 1 Maccabees 1:54), the Jews who gave in (Daniel 11:32), the teachers who held out (Daniel 11:33-35) and the "little help" (Daniel 11:34, often read as the Maccabean fighters) are all there. Daniel does not mention Judas Maccabeus by name.

uncommon: Daniel 11:34's "little help" is the Maccabean revolt (the reading of most critical scholars), described in cool terms.

sections.b: Most scholars read "a ruler of the covenant" in Daniel 11:22 as the high priest Onias III, deposed in 175 BC and murdered about 171 BC (2 Maccabees 4:7-10, 30-38). Jerome, following Porphyry, takes it as the Egyptian king Ptolemy VI. The identification is one of the main hinges of the critical reading of Daniel 9:26 as well.

Daniel 11:33-35 and 12:3, 10 speak of the maskilim, "those who have insight," who instruct the many and are cut down. Many scholars link them to the circle that produced Daniel and think they overlapped with the Hasideans of 1 Maccabees 2:42, though the book never uses the word Hasidean and its stance toward the Maccabean fighters ("a little help," 11:34) is cooler than 1 Maccabees' own.

Daniel 11:30 and 11:32 speak of Jews who "abandon the holy covenant" and who "act wickedly against the covenant", and who are won over by smooth words. They are the Hellenizers of 1 Maccabees 1:11-15 and 2 Maccabees 4:7-17, who built a gymnasium and took Greek ways. Daniel does not describe the new customs. It describes the choice.

Daniel 11:31 says the king's forces will profane the sanctuary, end the regular offering and set up the abomination that desolates. Daniel 12:11 dates the abomination 1,290 days from the removal of the regular offering. The Hebrew words differ in each passage: hashiqquts meshomem in 11:31, shiqquts shomem in 12:11, "on a wing of abominations comes one who makes desolate" in 9:27, and "the rebellion that desolates" in 8:13. In 1 Maccabees 1:54 "an abomination of desolation" was built on the altar on 15 Kislev, 167 BC. Jesus tells his disciples to watch for it again (Matthew 24:15; Mark 13:14), quoting the Greek rendering of Daniel. The phrase may be a mocking change of the Syrian title "Lord of heaven" (ba'al shamem) into "the abomination that desolates."

Daniel 12:7 repeats "a time, times and half a time" from Daniel 7:25. Daniel 12:11-12 adds 1,290 and 1,335 days, of which 1,290 is 1,260 plus thirty, and 1,335 is 1,290 plus forty-five. Maccabean readers count the Temple's profaning (167 BC) to its rededication (164 BC); year-day readers count years; futurist readers take them as literal days after the middle of a final seven. Jewish tradition warned against calculating (Sanhedrin 97b).

Daniel 12:2 is the clearest verse about individual resurrection in the Hebrew Bible. "Many" of those who sleep in the dusty ground will wake, some to life without end and some to shame, to a horror without end. Verse 3 promises the insightful and those who put the many in the right that they will shine like the sky and the stars. The Old Greek adds a third group. The verse is read as bodily resurrection by most Jews and Christians, as the resurrection of the martyrs and traitors of the persecution by Collins, and as national restoration by a few critics. The word "horror" occurs elsewhere only in Isaiah 66:24.

common: Daniel 12:2 teaches a bodily resurrection of the dead at the end.
uncommon: "Many" limits the resurrection to the martyrs and the traitors of the persecution (Collins, Nickelsburg).

sections.b: In Daniel 12:1 Michael "will stand up" at the time of distress as the great prince who stands guard over the sons of Daniel's people. He is the same figure as in Daniel 10:13, 21, where he helps the messenger against the prince of Persia. The Old Greek calls him "the great angel." Revelation 12:7 shows him fighting the dragon, and Jude 9 names him "the archangel." The Catholic and Orthodox churches keep feasts of Michael as an archangel. The Jehovah's Witnesses and Adventist writers, following Ellen White, identify him with Christ, and some older Protestant commentators, Matthew Henry among them, read Daniel 12:1 of Christ.

"Everyone found written in the scroll" will escape the time of distress (Daniel 12:1). The scroll belongs with the books opened in the judgment of Daniel 7:10 and with the older idea of God's record of his people (Exodus 32:32; Psalm 69:28; Isaiah 4:3; Malachi 3:16). Revelation calls it the book of life (Revelation 3:5; 20:12, 15).

sections.h: "A time of distress will come, with no equal" (Daniel 12:1)
sections.b: Daniel 12:1 describes a time of distress without equal since there was a nation. Jeremiah 30:7 uses the same kind of language, and Joel 2:2 describes the day of the LORD in it. Jesus repeats Daniel's wording in Matthew 24:21 and Mark 13:19. Readers differ: the persecution of 167-164 BC, the Roman war of AD 66-70, or a final tribulation.

Daniel 11:36-45 describes a king who does as he likes, raises himself above every god, speaks shocking things against the God of gods and meets his end between the seas and the holy mountain. Porphyry read it of Antiochus IV, Jerome says Christians read it of the Antichrist, and Rashi reads the kingdom of Rome. The Reformation churches read the pope into the figure (Westminster Confession 25.6), and dispensational teachers see a single future ruler. The closing verses do not match Antiochus' death in Persia in 164 BC.

sections.h: The teachers who fall and shine (Daniel 11:33-35; 12:3)
sections.b: Daniel 11:33-35 says the teachers with insight "will stumble, struck by sword and flame, taken captive and stripped of their goods" and that this refines and purifies them. Daniel 12:3 says they will shine like the stars. Scholars link the passage to Isaiah 52:13-53:12 and to the martyr stories of 2 Maccabees 6-7: the death of the faithful is not a defeat but the way to the shining.

In Daniel 11 Egypt is the "king of the south": the Ptolemies who held Judea until about 200 BC. The chapter follows their wars, marriages and defeats (Daniel 11:5-30) and ends with a king who takes Egypt's treasures, with Libyans and Cushites following him (Daniel 11:42-43).

Daniel 11:1-2 places Daniel's vision in the time of Darius the Mede and says that three more Persian kings will rise, the fourth richer than all and stirring up war on Greece. Most readers name Cambyses, Bardiya, Darius I and Xerxes. The Persian period is passed over in a verse; the Greek period gets the rest of the chapter.

sections.h: "The time of the end" in Daniel 11-12
sections.b: The phrase et qets, "the time of the end," is used in Daniel 8:17, 11:35, 11:40, 12:4 and 12:9. It marks the time of the final settling of the persecution. Whether it means 164 BC, the end of the age, or both is the main division of readers.

Daniel 10-12 has the marks of the apocalyptic style: a heavenly messenger, a long survey of history in the future tense, a time of distress, the resurrection and a command to seal the book. Unlike earlier prophets, the speaker says no "thus says the LORD"; the angel reveals what is written in the writing of truth (Daniel 10:21).

sections.h: Michael and the heavenly messenger in Daniel 10-12
sections.b: The angel in Daniel 10-12 speaks of the princes of Persia and Greece and of Michael, Daniel's prince (Daniel 10:13, 20-21). In Daniel 12:5-7 two others and the man in linen clothes appear at the river. Angels in Daniel are messengers, interpreters and guardians of nations.

Chapters 11-12 are the book's last vision. They carry the strongest link between the dating debate (the exact survey of 11:2-35 against the miss at 11:40-45), the resurrection (12:2-3) and the instruction to seal the book (12:4, 9). Daniel's last word is a personal promise: he will rest and will rise to his share at the end of the days (12:13).
